content: Once uploaded, the file can be embedded across all Wikimedia projects, unlike files uploaded directly to a specific project like Wikipedia, which are restricted to that project. Choose a descriptive and appropriate file name, as renaming is not possible after uploading. The file name must include the correct extension, and you can specify a destination filename during the upload process. Additionally, you can provide an upload summary. Each uploaded file is associated with an image description page, which includes the file name prefixed with Image: (or the equivalent namespace). File names are case-sensitive, including their extensions, except for the first character in most projects. When replacing an existing file on Commons, it is crucial to understand that all projects using that file will be affected. Therefore, the image description page on Commons should be linked to the local image pages of all projects using the file. When naming a file, use proper spacing and capitalization, as the name is visible in certain contexts, such as category pages. Avoid using a name already in use on any project unless the intention is to replace the existing file. Uploading files locally to a specific project has limitations. Such files cannot be used in other projects, and if a file with the same name exists on Commons, it becomes inaccessible for embedding in the local project. Local uploads should only be done for specific reasons, such as replacing a Commons file with a local version. To link to an uploaded file, use the Media: prefix for direct links to the file and the Image: prefix for links to the image description page. Piped links and interwiki linking styles work as usual. For non-image files, such as office documents, the media keyword is used, even though these files are not typically classified as media. Embedded internal images (from the same project or Commons) automatically link to their image description pages. These pages display the full image or a reduced version, depending on user preferences. Thumbnails can be added to articles using specific syntax, and their default width can be set in user preferences. Captions for thumbnails can include links, and both the image and an icon link to the image description page. The icon's hover text is Enlarge, even if the image on the description page is smaller than the thumbnail. Images can be positioned to the left or right of the text using specific syntax. Text will flow around the image unless a clear template is used to reset the text flow. Overlapping text or images can occur when floating text interacts with other elements. This can be mitigated by adding margins or using CSS adjustments. Images can also be displayed in tables or galleries. The gallery tag allows for quick thumbnail displays in columns, with captions and links. However, galleries have fixed image widths, and long captions may affect layout. Tables provide more control over image size, layout, and captions but require more effort to set up. Navigational maps can include clickable areas linked to pages. Tools like ImageMap and EasyTimeline allow for the creation of interactive images with defined map areas. These tools enable linking to internal or external pages based on user interaction with specific regions of the image. Use the Upload file link in the toolbox menu, select the file, and confirm that you are not violating copyrights. Preferred formats include JPEG for photographs, PNG for pixelated images, SVG for structured drawings, and OGG for audio. Descriptive file names are recommended to avoid confusion. Note that uploaded files can be edited or deleted by others if deemed necessary for the project. Replacing a file with the same name overwrites the existing file without warning. Changes to media files do not appear in the page history of articles using them but are recorded in the image description page's history and the upload log. To monitor changes, watch the upload log in addition to the article and image description pages. MediaWiki supports specific file types for upload, including PNG, JPEG, GIF, and OGG. Other file types, such as PDFs, can be enabled by modifying the LocalSettings.php file. File size limits may apply, and server settings like PHP's upload_max_size and Apache's LimitRequestBody can affect upload capabilities. Troubleshooting file uploads involves checking file integrity, extensions, and server settings. Corrupt files or unsupported extensions may cause errors.php is configured correctly for the desired file types, and verify that server limits are not restricting uploads. Templates can be used to display file links with appropriate icons. Revision histories of pages containing images reference the current versions of templates and images, not the versions at the time of the page's creation. Default settings may restrict embedding of certain images, and protection of an image page also protects the image itself. Embedding external images depends on project settings. If enabled, use unbracketed external link styles for inline images. For projects where embedding is disabled, download the image and upload it to Commons for use across all projects. External images are displayed in their actual size, and tables can be used to position images as needed. WikiTeX is a MediaWiki extension for creating graphs and diagrams. While not yet available on Wikimedia projects, it can be used on other MediaWiki installations to produce images for upload and embedding.
